n: Because Israel belongs to God as his children, they must not copy pagan mourning rituals like gashing the skin or shaving the front of the head for the dead.

f.g: Shaving the forehead as a mourning rite.

n: Israel is “holy” — set apart — and a “peculiar” people, meaning God’s own treasured possession. Their distinct way of life flows from that identity.

f.g: Hebrew segullah — a special treasure, not “odd.”

n: A summary rule introducing the food laws: do not eat anything God calls detestable.

f.g: Something ritually detestable or forbidden.

n: Domestic animals that could be eaten: cattle, sheep, and goats — the main livestock of Israel.

f.w: These are the beasts which ye shall eat

n: Wild animals that could also be eaten. The exact identities of some of these Hebrew names are uncertain; they were various deer, gazelles, ibex, and antelopes.

f.g: Probably a kind of antelope or ibex; the Hebrew word is uncertain.
Likely a wild sheep; true chamois do not live in Israel.

n: The general rule for land animals: they must have a split hoof and chew the cud. Both signs were needed.

f.g: Brings up partly digested food to chew again, like cows and sheep.

n: Animals with only one of the two signs were off-limits — like the camel, hare, and rock badger, which appear to chew but lack a true split hoof.

f.g: The rock hyrax, a small rabbit-like animal living among rocks.
Rabbits move their jaws as if chewing cud, so they were classed this way.

n: The pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud, so it was unclean — not to be eaten or even touched when dead.
Water creatures could be eaten if they had both fins and scales — like most ordinary fish.
Creatures without fins and scales — such as shellfish, eels, and catfish — were unclean.
Birds in general were allowed unless they were on the forbidden list that follows.

f.g: Such as doves, pigeons, quail, and chickens.

n: The forbidden birds begin with large birds of prey. Most were scavengers or hunters that ate carrion or blood.

f.g: “Bone-breaker”; probably the bearded vulture.
Osprey; possibly a type of vulture.

n: More birds of prey. Translators are often unsure which exact species are meant.

f.g: An old word for a kite (a hawk-like bird); the Hebrew may name a different bird.
Including related species.

n: Ravens and crows, which eat carrion, were unclean.
Owls and other night or predatory birds are listed. The “cuckow” likely refers to a seabird such as a gull.

f.g: Old spelling of cuckoo; the Hebrew may mean a gull or sea bird.

n: Various owls, and another bird the KJV calls a swan — possibly a water hen or another owl.

f.g: The Hebrew word is uncertain; possibly an owl or water hen.

n: Water birds and more scavengers. These creatures fed on fish or dead animals.

f.g: An old name for a vulture.

n: The stork, heron, hoopoe, and bat close the list. Ancient people grouped the bat with flying creatures.

f.g: Probably the hoopoe, a crested bird.

n: Most winged insects were unclean. Leviticus allows certain locusts as an exception.
Repeating the rule: any clean flying creature may be eaten.

f.g: Fowls = birds or flying creatures.

n: Israel must not eat an animal that died naturally. Such meat could be given or sold to non-Israelites. And never boil a young goat in its mother’s milk — a pagan practice and a cruelty the law avoided.

f.w: any thing that dieth of itself
seethe a kid in his mother's milk
f.g: Seethe = boil. The basis for the Jewish rule separating meat and dairy.

n: Now the tithe: a tenth of each year’s harvest was to be set apart for the Lord. Latter-day Saints today live a law of tithing too.

f.g: A tenth.

n: This tithe was eaten in a sacred meal at the sanctuary. Its purpose: to teach Israel to reverence God continually.

f.w: that thou mayest learn to fear the LORD
f.g: Regular giving trains the heart to honor God.

n: God made allowance for distance. If the sanctuary was too far to haul crops and animals,…

f.w: if the way be too long for thee

n: …they could sell the tithe produce, carry the money to the sanctuary, and spend it there.

f.w: bind up the money in thine hand
f.g: Tie the silver in a bundle to carry it.

n: At the sanctuary they could buy whatever food and drink they wanted and hold a joyful feast before the Lord with their household.

f.g: Fermented drink such as beer; the law of Moses permitted it. Latter-day Saints follow the later Word of Wisdom (D&C 89).

n: The Levites must be included in the feast, since they owned no land of their own.
Every third year the tithe was handled differently: it was stored in the local town instead of being taken to the sanctuary.

f.w: At the end of three years

n: That third-year tithe fed the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Caring for the poor brings God’s blessing on all one’s work.

f.w: the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow
